issues.legal_issue: A valid certificate permitting an appeal does not confine the Supreme Court’s consideration to the questions identified in the certificate.
material_facts: The High Court granted a certificate under Article 133, identifying substantial questions about whether a will could effect a severance in status and whether related pleas could be raised for the first time on appeal.
The respondent argued that the certificate prevented the appellants from challenging findings on adoption and partition.
issues.conclusion: Once a certificate satisfying Article 133 is validly granted, the Supreme Court may consider the correctness of the decision on questions of fact or law beyond those specified in the certificate.
issues.legal_principle: Article 133 makes a qualifying High Court certificate a condition for maintaining the appeal, but does not restrict the scope of the appeal once the certificate is valid. A successful party may still challenge the maintainability of an appeal on the ground that the certificate was improperly issued.

predicates.appeal_to_supreme_court_is_brought_under: A party brings an appeal to the Supreme Court under a certificate that satisfies the applicable requirements.

issues.definition: When an appeal is brought under a valid certificate, the Supreme Court may review the decision beyond the questions specified in that certificate.

issues.legal_issue: Concurrent findings of fact are ordinarily not disturbed on appeal unless exceptional circumstances warrant intervention.
material_facts: The trial court and the High Court both found that the alleged adoption and partition had not been proved.

The Supreme Court examined the appellants’ criticisms of the evidence and concluded that the findings were supported by evidence and did not involve exceptional injustice or a relevant procedural or legal error.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to interfere with the concurrent findings of fact.
issues.legal_principle: The Court followed the established practice of ordinarily leaving concurrent findings based on relevant evidence undisturbed, while retaining power to intervene in exceptional cases, including where findings shock the Court’s conscience, legal process has been disregarded, natural justice has been violated, or substantial and grave injustice has otherwise occurred. The Court referred to Rani v. Khagendra, Fatima Bibi v. Ahmed Bakshi, Harendra v. Haridasi, Bibhabati v. Ramendra, Nanalal v. Bombay Life Assurance Co., Firm Srinivas Ram v. Mahabir Prasad, Trojan & Co. v. Naganna, Rajinder Chand v. Mst. Sukhi, Bhikka v. Charan Singh, M.M.B. Catholicos v. P. Paulo Avira, and Narayan Bhagwantrao Gosavi Balajiwale v. Gopal Vinayak Gosavi.

predicates.appeal_challenges_concurrent_findings_of: A party asks an appellate court to reconsider factual findings reached by both lower courts.
predicates.findings_show_exceptional_injustice_or_s: The concurrent findings disclose exceptional injustice, disregard of legal process, or a violation of natural justice.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges concurrent factual findings and they disclose no exceptional injustice or serious procedural error, those findings are left undisturbed.

issues.legal_issue: The legal burden of proving a fact remains on the party asserting it, although the evidentiary onus may shift during the evaluation of evidence.
material_facts: The appellants relied on evidence they said supported adoption and partition, including old transactions, documents, admissions, and conduct.
The Court held that those circumstances could affect the evidentiary onus but did not alter the appellants’ burden to prove the adoption and partition on which their claim depended.
issues.conclusion: The appellants retained the burden of proving adoption and partition; the onus of producing or answering evidence could shift as the evidence was evaluated.
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished the burden of proof, which remains on the person required to prove a fact, from the onus of proof, which may shift continuously during the evaluation of evidence. It held that circumstances affecting the weight of evidence do not change the incidence of the legal burden.

predicates.a_party_asserts_a_fact_as_the_basis_for_: A party relies on an asserted fact as a basis for obtaining relief.
predicates.evidentiary_onus_shifts_during_evaluatio: The evidentiary onus shifts as the court assesses the evidence and circumstances in the case.

issues.definition: When a party relies on a fact to obtain relief, shifts in the evidentiary onus do not transfer that party’s legal burden of proving the fact.

issues.legal_issue: A party seeking to displace natural succession by alleging an adoption must prove the fact and validity of the adoption.
material_facts: The appellants alleged that a child had been adopted by a family member, thereby affecting the succession to property.
The trial court and the High Court disbelieved the witnesses supporting the alleged adoption and found the documentary record and subsequent conduct inconsistent or inconclusive.
The Supreme Court found no exceptional basis to disturb those concurrent findings.
issues.conclusion: The alleged adoption was not established, and the appellants failed to discharge their burden of proving its fact and validity.
issues.legal_principle: A person seeking to displace natural succession by alleging adoption bears the burden of proving both the factum and validity of the adoption. The Court applied the general distinction between the fixed burden of proof and a shifting evidentiary onus.

predicates.adoption_claimed_to_displace_natural_suc: A party alleges an adoption as a basis for changing the ordinary course of succession to property.
predicates.claimant_failed_to_prove_the_fact_and_va: The party alleging adoption did not establish that the adoption occurred and was valid.

issues.definition: If a party relies on an alleged adoption to displace natural succession but fails to prove that the adoption occurred and was valid, the adoption is not established.

issues.legal_issue: A party asserting partition must prove it, and a family is presumed joint unless the contrary is established.
material_facts: The appellants claimed that the family property had been partitioned, including a division between two family members, but did not produce partition lists, accounts, pattas, or receipts said to exist.
The oral and documentary evidence did not establish the asserted division between those family members.
Both lower courts found that the claimed partition had not been proved.
issues.conclusion: The asserted partition between the family members was not established, and the Supreme Court declined to disturb the concurrent factual finding.
issues.legal_principle: A Hindu family is presumed joint unless the contrary is proved, and the party asserting a particular partition bears the burden of proving it. Whether partition occurred is a question of fact. The Court relied on Bhagavati Prasad Shah v. Dulhin Rameshwari Juar, which explains that separation of one coparcener does not itself create a presumption either way about whether the remaining coparceners also separated; the issue depends on the evidence and the intention of the parties.

predicates.a_party_claims_a_partition: A party relies on an alleged division of family property as the basis for relief.
predicates.family_is_presumed_joint: The family is treated as joint unless evidence establishes otherwise.
predicates.claimant_failed_to_prove_the_asserted_pa: The party asserting partition did not establish that the claimed division occurred.

issues.definition: When a party asserts a partition but fails to prove it, the family remains treated as joint and the asserted partition is not established.

issues.legal_issue: A member of a joint Hindu family effects severance in status through a definite and unequivocal intention to separate that is brought to the knowledge of the affected family members.
material_facts: A family member executed a will that the appellants relied on as a declaration of an intention to separate.

There were only two relevant members of the joint family for the issue, and the appellants did not establish that the surviving member or his guardian knew the contents of the will before the testator died.
The guardian’s presence inside the house when the will was executed did not establish knowledge of its contents.
issues.conclusion: An uncommunicated declaration does not effect severance in status; the declaration must reach the person or persons affected by an appropriate process.
issues.legal_principle: A member of a joint Hindu family may unilaterally separate by a definite and unequivocal declaration of an intention to hold a share separately, but the declaration must be communicated to the affected members. The Court relied on Hindu law texts, including the Mitakshara, Saraswati Vilasa, Viramitrodaya, and Vyavahara Mayukha, and on Suraj Narain v. Iqbal Narain, Girija Bai v. Sadashiv Dhundiraj, Kawal Nain v. Budh Singh, Ramalinga Annavi v. Narayana Annavi, Sayed Kasam v. Jorawar Singh, Soundararayan v. Arunachalam Chetty, Bal Krishna v. Ram Krishna, Babu Ramasaray Prasad Choudhary v. Radhika Devi, Kamepalli Avilamma v. Mannem Venkataswamy, and Adujallath Kathusumma v. Adujalath Beechu. The Court rejected the contrary approach in Narayana Rao v. Purushothama Rao and did not accept it insofar as Indira v. Sivaprasada Rao followed that approach.

predicates.joint_family_member_makes_a_definite_une: A member of a joint family clearly and unequivocally expresses an intention to separate and hold a share separately.
predicates.affected_member_does_not_learn_of_it_bef: The family member affected by the declaration does not learn of it before the person making it dies.

issues.definition: A definite and unequivocal separation declaration does not effect severance before the declarant’s death if the affected member does not learn of it during the declarant’s lifetime.

issues.legal_issue: When a communicated declaration of separation relates back to its expression, intervening rights that have vested in others remain protected.
material_facts: The Court considered the relationship between the date a family member expressed an intention to separate and the later date when that intention became known to the affected member.
It held that the doctrine of relation back could not disturb rights accruing to others in the family property between those dates.
In this case, the affected member did not learn of the will’s contents before the declarant died, so the other member’s interest devolved on the declarant’s death.
issues.conclusion: Once the affected member learns of the declaration, severance relates back to the date of its expression, but rights that vested in others in the interval are preserved.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the doctrine of relation back by analogy to the doctrine recognized in adoption law, while limiting its retroactive effect to protect vested rights. It reasoned that retroactivity does not ordinarily unsettle vested rights and that equity and certainty of title require those rights to be saved.

predicates.separation_declaration_is_communicated_t: A declaration of intention to separate is brought to the knowledge of the family member affected by it.
predicates.rights_vest_in_others_before_communicati: Another person acquires a vested right in family property after the declaration is expressed but before it is communicated.

issues.definition: When a separation declaration is communicated, severance relates back to its expression, but rights that vested in others before communication remain protected.

issues.legal_issue: A will by an undivided member does not itself effect severance and cannot dispose of that member’s undivided interest in joint family property.
material_facts: A family member executed a will disposing of property that the appellants claimed belonged to him as a separate share.
The alleged earlier partition had not been proved.
The will’s contents were not shown to have been known to the affected family member or his guardian before the testator died.
issues.conclusion: The will did not convey the testator’s interest in the joint family property because it was not established that he had become separated before his death.
issues.legal_principle: A will speaks from the testator’s death. An undivided coparcener may execute a will, but cannot validly bequeath an undivided interest in joint family property; the bequest can operate only if the testator was separated before death. A will may be relied on to ascertain an intention to separate, but the declaration must be communicated to the affected member before the testator dies for severance to occur in time to prevent devolution by survivorship.

predicates.a_will_disposes_of_an_undivided_joint_fa: A will purports to dispose of a family member’s interest in property held jointly by an undivided family.
predicates.testator_was_not_proved_separate_before_: The evidence does not establish that the testator became separate from the family before dying.

issues.definition: A will does not convey an undivided joint-family interest when the testator’s separation before death is not established.
